author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “they will not be well pleased. I cannot expect mercy at their hands, whether I succeed or fail; and if I should fail, they will not inquire whether the failure is owing to my own incapacity, to the blameless errors to which we are all liable, to the faults or mistakes of others, to the deficiency of our means, […]”
sourceTitle: To To the Earl of Liverpool, Pombal, 1810-06-02
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Busaco eve resolve: no mercy expected, none asked.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Increased Difficulty or Position. I certainly feel every day more and more the difficulty of the situation in which I am placed. I am obliged to be everywhere, and if absent from any operation something goes wrong. […]”
sourceTitle: To To the Earl of Liverpool, Villa Formosa, 1811-05-15
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Fuentes d'Oñoro aftermath: details win battles.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Gallantry or Troops. It is impossible that any expressions of mine can convey to your Lordship the sense which I entertain of the gallantry of the officers and troops upon this occasion. […]”
sourceTitle: To To the Earl of Liverpool, Camp before Badajoz, 1812-04-07
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Badajoz stormed: gallantry beyond expression.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Public Traducers. All those who serve the public honestly and faithfully have for their enemies and traducers those who are desirous of profiting by the public wants, incon veniences and disasters, and by the misfortunes of the times.”
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Contractors and traducers: the army's parasites.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “s than OFFICERS. 73 to the instruction we have given them. In the end of last campaign, they behaved, in many instances, exceedingly ill, because they were in extreme misery, the Portuguese government having neglected to pay them. […]”
sourceTitle: To To the Earl of Liverpool, Lesaca, 1813-07-25
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Portuguese paid, Portuguese fight: regularity wins.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “s than 6,000 sick and wounded, who were captured in the town in little more than a week by Gen. Trant. The battle of Toulouse had no resemblance to the battle of Busaco. M. Choumara's readers will judge which party won it. […]”
sourceTitle: To To tike Minister at War, Madrid, Toulouse, 1814-04-14
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Toulouse taken; Buonaparte overturned.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Procuring Intelligence. There is a good deal of charlatanisme in what is called procuring intelligence, as there is in everything else.”
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Intelligence charlatans, Brussels, May 1815.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Remains of the French Army. The remains of the French army have retired upon Laon. All accounts agree in stating that it is in a very wretched state, and that in addition to its losses in battle and in prisoners, it is losing vast numbers of men by desertion. […]”
sourceTitle: To To Earl Bathurst, Le Cateau, 1815-06-22
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: French army dissolving after Waterloo.

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “Continuing Operations. I could not consider Buonaparte's abdication of a usurped power in favour of his son, and his handing over the Government provisionally to five persons named by himself, to be that description of security which the Allies had in view, which should induce them to lay down their arms, […]”
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: No laying down arms: abdication insufficient security.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Abolit ten o'clock, the Emperor entered my apartment; lie came imawares, as he wished to take a walk. I followed him, and he walked for some time towards the wood, where \ve were taken up by the calash. A considérable interval had elapsed since he made use of it. […]”
sourceTitle: Las Cases, Mémorial (English ed., 1823), Fifth Part conversations
archive: Las Cases, Journal of Napoleon's St Helena conversations (London, 1823) — public domain
context: July 10, 1816, dated in print: walk, calash, Beaumarchais read. Reported speech via Las Cases' journal; undated in print except where stated.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Rostopchin baving been pronounced, I presumed to remark, that tbe colour at that time given to bis patriotic action, bad very much surprized me, for he bad interested me instead of exciting my indignation, and even much more, that I bad envied bim!. […]”
sourceTitle: Las Cases, Mémorial (English ed., 1823), Fifth Part conversations
archive: Las Cases, Journal of Napoleon's St Helena conversations (London, 1823) — public domain
context: On Moscow's burning and Rostopchin; undated conversation, 1816. Reported speech via Las Cases' journal; undated in print except where stated.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Blucher and the Duke of Wellington were surprized; they saw nothing, knew nothing, of the opérations which were carrying on near their advanced posts. '* In order to attack the two hostile armies, the French mioht hâve out-flanked their rio-ht or left, or penetrated their centre. […]”
sourceTitle: Las Cases, Mémorial (English ed., 1823), Fifth Part conversations
archive: Las Cases, Journal of Napoleon's St Helena conversations (London, 1823) — public domain
context: Dictated Waterloo narrative: the surprise opening. Reported speech via Las Cases' journal; undated in print except where stated.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Quatre-Bras, to take up a position there at the break of day, and even to entrench himself; he hesitated, and lost eiglit hours. The Prince of Orange, with onl}»- 9000 men, retained, on the IGth until three o'clock in the afternoon, that important position. […]”
sourceTitle: Las Cases, Mémorial (English ed., 1823), Fifth Part conversations

displayText: “position at SaintJean d'Acre, he observed: — *' The position which I occupied in the middle *' of Syria, with 12,000 men only, was, it must be " admitted, a very enterprizing measure. I was *' at the distance of 500 leagues from Desaix, who *' formed the other extremity of my army. […]”
sourceTitle: Las Cases, Mémorial (English ed., 1823), Fifth Part conversations

author: W. Warden
displayText: “3d of August, 1815, his Majesty's ship Northumberland J Captain Ross, bearing the flag of Admiral Sir George Cockburn, who was selected by Government for this important duty, weighed anchor from Spithead, and, after having contended with adverse winds, came within sight of the Berry-head, a head-land forming the extremity of Torbay, […]”
archive: Warden, Letters from the Northumberland and St Helena (London, 1816) — public domain
context: Transfer Bellerophon to Northumberland; date from narrative.

author: W. Warden
displayText: “14th of October, 1815, shot out a parting ray e'er it sunk beneath the horizon. Under this small illumined space, was obscurely perceived the lofty Peak of Saint Helena.— The memorable morning soon dawned which was to usher in the commencement of Napoleons exile. This new feature in his history will be the subject of my next Letter. &c. […]”
archive: Warden, Letters from the Northumberland and St Helena (London, 1816) — public domain
context: Landfall eve: the Peak sighted at sunset; narrative date explicit.

author: W. Warden
displayText: “voluntary surrender of the Exemperor of France and his suite, with bag and baggage, on board the Bellerophon, To have taken the ship on which he might have attempted to make his escape, was a natural expectation, as it would have been a probable event; […]”
archive: Warden, Letters from the Northumberland and St Helena (London, 1816) — public domain
context: The surrender that surprised Maitland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The English will be obliged to re-embark in a few days. Pichegru is preparing to pass the Rhine. La Vendee is tranquil, and the Chouans are only seen north of the Loire. Peace with Spain is imminent. " The Dutch appear warm friends of their Revolution. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Quiberon landings; Pichegru about to cross the Rhine.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am a General employed in the army of the West; my malady detains me here. I await further details from you. I believe you avoid speaking to me about Desire on purpose, &c.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Unemployed general, sick in Paris, awaiting fate.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I congratulate you on joining the army Fortune, favour, and the esteem of men vary and oscillate perpetually I have been appointed to serve in the army of La Vendee as General of the Line: I have not accepted, A great many ofificers would command a brigade better than I could; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Fortune varies: angling for employment.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “No matter what happens, you need feel no alarm concerning me, as I have for friends the best men of all parties. Mariette is extremely zealous in my behalf: you are aware of his opinions. I am on intimate terms with Doulcet You know my other friends of an opposite opinion. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Convention renewed; Vendémiaire brewing.

author: The Executive Directory
displayText: “16 Ventose, year 4 [March 6, 1796]. The Executive Directory addresses to you herewith, eitizen-general, the instructions which it has drawn up for the conduct of the ensuing campaign in Italy. […]”
archive: Secret letters from Napoleon's cabinet (London, 1846), Vol. I — public domain
context: The Directory's Italy instructions: seize Savona if useful; spare Genoa. Incoming voice: Paris orders to its general.

author: The Executive Directory
displayText: “29 Messidor, year 4 [July 17, 1796). According to the last despatches from the general-inchief of the army of the Alps, citizen-general, it appears that he had not received the 200,000 francs in money which you have been charged to send him. […]”
sourceTitle: To the General-in-Chief: reply on Mantua, 1796-07-17
archive: Secret letters from Napoleon's cabinet (London, 1846), Vol. I — public domain
context: Paris answers Roverbella: Mantua's supplies will decide. Incoming voice: Paris orders to its general.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter, good little Josephine. I perceived with sorrow that you suffered from the journey. But a few days of repose will do much for you, I am very well, indeed. I went yesterday to the hunt at Marly,1 and wounded myself very slightly in one finger, in shooting a boar. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Malmaison summer: health anxieties.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 29th of June. You do not speak of your health, or of the effect of the baths. I see that you intend to be on your return in eight days. That will afford great pleasure to your friend, who wearies of being alone. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: 29 June letter answered; health unwritten.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I arrived yesterday, at five o'clock in the evening, at Dresden, in very good health, although I have been a hundred hours in the carriage without leaving it. I am here at the house of the King of Saxony, with whom I am very much pleased. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Printed 1801 in error; Dresden stay was July 1807 on the Tilsit return.
